summary: BBC News reports a death toll of 53 with 76 rescued as of 22:00 GMT Tuesday 21 July, attributed to Prime Minister Mark Phillips, and 179 aboard against a manifest of 116 passengers and 17 crew. It states a distress call came at 23:01 local time, that the captain and a crew member were in custody after positive cannabis tests, and that the French army sent 12 divers, two doctors and a mechanic. Survivor Elena Moonsammy's account, given to Kiskadee Watch, describes the ferry tilting after a large wave.

Reuters, datelined Georgetown 20 July, states the government reported 27 bodies recovered from a ferry that capsized with 179 aboard, and attributes to the National Communications Network figures of 69 rescued and 83 missing as of Monday afternoon. It gives the search area as 1,040 sq km, against 1,070 in the Guardian, and attributes to Minister Deodat Indar that private company VEHSI, Exxon Mobil and local fishermen located the wreck. It notes the captain and another crew member were in custody after positive marijuana tests.

The Guardian, reporting from Essequibo on 20 July, states two deaths were confirmed and a criminal investigation had begun. It attributes to Minister Juan Edghill that the manifest was wrong, only 35 of 67 rescued appearing on it, and that the vessel was certified for 397 passengers and 284 tonnes of cargo, with 250 lifejackets, two lifeboats and six inflatable rafts. It gives the search area as expanded from 400 to 1,070 sq km, against 1,040 in Reuters. Survivor Adam Matabheek describes the vessel leaning hours beforehand.

Deutsche Welle attributes to Prime Minister Mark Phillips on 20 July at least 27 dead, 83 missing and 69 rescued from a vessel carrying around 180 people. It states air traffic control received a distress call around 23:00 local time on Saturday, and gives the rescued as 41 men, 11 women, six boys and nine girls. It attributes to Phillips that the captain and mate survived and returned to assist, that the vessel had maintenance in 2024, and was licensed for more than 300 passengers.

CBC News, publishing Thomson Reuters copy on 20 July, gives 27 bodies recovered from a vessel carrying 179 people, with 69 rescued and 83 missing as of Monday afternoon per the National Communications Network, and a search area of 1,040 sq km, against the Guardian's 1,070. It states air traffic control received a distress call around 23:00 on Saturday. It attributes to Minister Edghill that darkness and a lack of scanner-equipped vessels hampered response. Survivor Leon Murray, quoted from Ignite News, states six of his relatives were not found.

The MV Barima entry is a collaboratively edited encyclopedia article, not original reporting. The 26 July version gives the vessel as Guyana-flagged, launched 9 May 1939, with capacity for 394 passengers and 18 crew and carrying 250 life jackets, six inflatable life rafts and two rigid life rafts. It states departure about 15:15 with 179 aboard, capsizing around 23:00 after a large wave, and 73 bodies recovered, 76 rescued and 30 missing by 24 July. Its lede's '162 passengers and 17 crew' does not match 179 used elsewhere.
